result.headline: ADR 0002's mechanism is right and its conclusion is right, but the stated consequence is WRONG: the relationship view does rank pairs by effective timestamp and keep only open rows, but the rank is PARTITION BY <src>_key, type_key, so a changed foreign key never drops the child out of the view — it silently re-points every one of that child's rows at the NEW parent and erases the old pair. Verified: after CH1 moved P1->P2, the pair table held BOTH rows (both row_st='Y') and the view held CH1|P2 only. The real reason to read the pair table is history, not disappearance. Separately, ADR 0002's supporting claim that "view_<entity>_with_rel carries no relationship key columns at all" is only true on the relationship's SOURCE side; on the TARGET side it carries the source entity's key AND all its attributes, fanned out — sum(CHILD_AMOUNT) over view_PARENT_with_rel was 200.75 against a true 150.75.
objects: dab.CHILD_PARENT_x — BASE TABLE. The pair table. Named <SRC>_<TGT>_x from the entity pair, NOT from the relationship name; a second relationship between the same two entities would land in this same table, distinguished only by type_key.
dab.view_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT — VIEW, named view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>. Body is literally `SELECT * FROM dab.f_child_parent_x();` — no type_key predicate.
dab.v_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT — VIEW, named v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>. The raw pair table INNER JOINed to dab__meta.atom_contx_desc to add a rel_name column; no ranking, no row_st filter.

dab.f_CHILD_PARENT_x — DuckDB TABLE MACRO (invisible to information_schema.tables; only duckdb_functions() shows it). Takes p_eff_tmstp with a default, so it is point-in-time capable: f_child_parent_x(TIMESTAMP '2026-01-15') returned CH1|P1 while f_child_parent_x() returned CH1|P2.

dab.f_PARENT_WITH_REL — TABLE MACRO that a relationship MUTATES rather than creates. With no relationship it is a passthrough (verified against the repo's slice-1 warehouse: f_ORDER_WITH_REL is `SELECT f_ORDER.ORDER_key, ... FROM dab.f_order(p_eff_tmstp)`). Once the entity is a relationship TARGET it becomes a double LEFT JOIN through the pair macro to the source entity, so view_PARENT_with_rel gains CHILD_key, CHILD_CODE, CHILD_AMOUNT, CHILD_PLACED_ON and fans out.
dab.f_CHILD_WITH_REL — TABLE MACRO, unchanged passthrough. The relationship's SOURCE side gains nothing; view_CHILD_with_rel is byte-identical to view_CHILD.

dab__meta.atom_contx_desc — gains one row, ('1','CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT'), mapping the relationship id to the type_key used in the pair table. atom_contx_key is VARCHAR, type_key is BIGINT, so a lookup needs CAST (the engine's own v_* view does exactly that).

NOT created by a relationship: the dab__stage relx2_load/relx2_reader/relx2_delta/relx2_integration/relx2_target staging tables already exist in the repo's relationship-free slice-1 warehouse — install/deploy makes them regardless.

Baseline for the diff: slice 1 (one entity, no relationship) has exactly BASE TABLE ORDER_desc/ORDER_focal/ORDER_idfr, VIEW v_ORDER_desc/view_ORDER/view_ORDER_hist/view_ORDER_with_rel, MACRO f_ORDER/f_ORDER_WITH_REL. My two-entity+one-relationship model added exactly 4 dab objects on top of the per-entity set: CHILD_PARENT_x, view_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT, v_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT, f_CHILD_PARENT_x.
result.relationshipView:
The real name is dab.view_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT — i.e. view_<SOURCE>_<RELATIONSHIP NAME>_<TARGET>, with the model's casing preserved. There is a SECOND view, v_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT (v_ prefix), which is a different object.

CREATE VIEW dab.view_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT AS SELECT * FROM dab.f_child_parent_x();

DESCRIBE dab."view_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT"
  CHILD_key                VARCHAR
  PARENT_key               VARCHAR
  type_key                 BIGINT
  eff_tmstp                TIMESTAMP
  ver_tmstp                TIMESTAMP

SELECT * FROM dab."view_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT"  -- 6 rows, final state
CHILD_key | PARENT_key | type_key | eff_tmstp | ver_tmstp
CH1 | P2 | 1 | 2026-02-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:26:33.824411
CH2 | P2 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568
CH3 | P3 | 1 | 2026-03-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:27:20.904874
CH4 | P1 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568
CH5 | P1 | 1 | 2026-04-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:27:42.891238
CH5 | P2 | 1 | 2026-04-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:27:42.891238

The macro behind it, verbatim from duckdb_functions().macro_definition — this is the ADR's "ranks pairs and keeps the open rows", and it is exactly right about the mechanism:

SELECT CHILD_key, PARENT_key, type_key, eff_tmstp, ver_tmstp
FROM (SELECT CHILD_key, PARENT_key, type_key, eff_tmstp, ver_tmstp, row_st,
             rank() OVER (PARTITION BY CHILD_key, type_key
                          ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC) AS nbr
      FROM dab.CHILD_PARENT_x
      WHERE (eff_tmstp <= CAST(p_eff_tmstp AS TIMESTAMP))) AS A
WHERE ((nbr = 1) AND (row_st = 'Y'))

The other view, dab.v_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT, is the RAW pair table plus a name — no rank, no row_st filter:
CREATE VIEW dab.v_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT AS SELECT an.CHILD_key, an.PARENT_key, bn.val_str AS rel_name, an.eff_tmstp, an.ver_tmstp, an.row_st, an.data_key, an.inst_key, an.inst_row_key, an.popln_tmstp FROM dab.CHILD_PARENT_x AS an INNER JOIN dab__meta.atom_contx_desc AS bn ON ((an.type_key = CAST(bn.atom_contx_key AS BIGINT)));
DESCRIBE gives: CHILD_key VARCHAR | PARENT_key VARCHAR | rel_name VARCHAR | eff_tmstp TIMESTAMP | ver_tmstp TIMESTAMP | row_st VARCHAR | data_key BIGINT | inst_key BIGINT | inst_row_key BIGINT | popln_tmstp TIMESTAMP
and it returned all 4 pair rows (including both CH1 rows) at the point where the ranked view returned 3.
result.changedForeignKey:
TEST: CH1 loaded pointing at P1 with extracted_at 2026-01-01. Then a second das__staged row for CH1 pointing at P2 with extracted_at 2026-02-01 (append, FULL_LOG — exactly how DAS lands a change). `daana-cli execute` re-run, exit 0.

BEFORE — pair TABLE dab.CHILD_PARENT_x, 3 rows:
CH1 | P1 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568 | Y
CH2 | P2 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568 | Y
CH4 | P1 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568 | Y
BEFORE — relationship VIEW, the same 3 rows.

AFTER — pair TABLE dab.CHILD_PARENT_x, 4 rows, BOTH CH1 rows present, BOTH row_st='Y':
CH1 | P1 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568 | Y
CH1 | P2 | 1 | 2026-02-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:26:33.824411 | Y
CH2 | P2 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568 | Y
CH4 | P1 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568 | Y

AFTER — relationship VIEW dab.view_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT, 3 rows:
CH1 | P2 | 1 | 2026-02-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:26:33.824411
CH2 | P2 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568
CH4 | P1 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568

VERDICT. ADR 0002 says: "those views rank pairs by effective timestamp and keep the open rows ... so a changed foreign key can drop out of the view entirely — rows silently missing from the bridge, with the query still running and the total merely smaller." The first half is CONFIRMED verbatim by the macro SQL. The second half is WRONG. CH1 did not drop out. The rank partitions by (CHILD_key, type_key) and every pair row is row_st='Y', so every child that has ever had any pair keeps exactly one row in the view. Nothing goes missing and no total shrinks.

What actually happens is worse in a quieter way, and it is the real argument for reading the table: the OLD pair is erased from the view. Every bridge row for CH1 — including a January event that happened while CH1 belonged to P1 — would be attributed to P2. The failure mode is misattribution, not omission; the count stays right and the grouping goes wrong.

I looked for any path that DOES drop a child out. There is exactly one, and it is not a foreign-key change: if the child's SOURCE ROW disappears from das__staged entirely, FULL_LOG's truedelta DEL branch writes a second pair row with the same eff_tmstp, a later ver_tmstp and row_st='N', which the macro's `nbr=1 AND row_st='Y'` then filters out. Reproduced in a copy of the probe by deleting CH4 from das__raw:
CH4 | P1 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:25:15.586568 | Y
CH4 | P1 | 1 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 2026-09-07 22:31:07.086818 | N
CH4 then vanished from view_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT — and from view_CHILD as well, so the entity goes with it; this is a whole-row soft delete, not a silently-dropped key. In this architecture das__staged is append-only over dlt parquet, so a source row cannot disappear and this path is unreachable.

The engine's own source comment (extracted from the daana-cli binary, template "TWO_WAY_X_RELATION Complex Reader") states the design explicitly:
"DAANA-131: Reader emits Y rows only [—] the previous UNION-ALL N-arm (close rows at next_eff_tmstp - 1s) is removed ... Set transitions are handled at the view layer via set-oriented RANK partition (PARTITION BY focal01_key, type_key [—] see ADR-110). FULL_LOG retains its source-row-disappearance soft-delete via the truedelta's DEL CASE branch [—] that emission is separate from the reader and unchanged."

So: ADR 0002's decision (read the pair table, not the view) stands. Its stated reason does not. The sentence "a changed foreign key can drop out of the view entirely — rows silently missing from the bridge" should be replaced with something like "the view keeps only the newest pair per child, so a changed foreign key rewrites history: every past event of that child is re-attributed to the new parent."
result.orphanChild:
A child with no parent appears in NEITHER the pair table nor the relationship view. It appears normally in view_CHILD and view_CHILD_with_rel, and it does not appear in view_PARENT_with_rel at all.

CH6, loaded with parent_code NULL:
  dab.view_CHILD                   : [('CH6','CH6',Decimal('60.00000000'),datetime(2026,1,6,0,0))]
  dab.CHILD_PARENT_x (pair TABLE)  : []
  dab.view_CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT : []
  dab.view_CHILD_with_rel          : [('CH6','CH6',Decimal('60.00000000'),datetime(2026,1,6,0,0))]
  dab.view_PARENT_with_rel         : []

The cause is in the engine's reader template, which filters the pair source with
  AND CAST('p_focal02_idfr_param' AS {{STRING}}) IS NOT NULL
so a NULL foreign key produces no pair row rather than a pair row with a NULL key.

Consequence for the generator: the ONLY evidence that a child is parentless is the ABSENCE of a row. The join from the child to the pair objects must be LEFT — which matches ADR 0002's rule "a join on an inherited key must be LEFT". Measured: 6 children, LEFT JOIN keeps 6 distinct children, INNER JOIN keeps 5.

A NULLED-OUT foreign key is NOT retracted. CH2 was loaded pointing at P2 (extracted_at 2026-01-01), then re-landed with parent_code NULL at extracted_at 2026-03-01 and re-executed. Nothing was written: the pair table still holds only CH2|P2|2026-01-01|Y and the view still shows CH2|P2. There is no tombstone and no row_st flip. The relationship is append-only and cannot express "this child no longer belongs to anyone" — the stale pair survives forever. (Conversely, an orphan that LATER gains a parent does get a pair row, dated by the load in which it first pointed somewhere: CH3 got CH3|P3|2026-03-01|Y.)
result.cardinality:
No. The model cannot declare cardinality, and this is settled by the engine's own error message rather than inferred.

Adding `cardinality: MANY_TO_ONE` to the relationship is rejected by both `check model` and `lint`:
  Invalid field 'cardinality' in relationship 'BELONGS_TO'. Valid fields are: name, definition, description, source, target, source_entity_id, target_entity_id, type

That list is the whole grammar. `source`/`target` are alternate spellings of `source_entity_id`/`target_entity_id` (the binary also carries `target_entity_ids` for N-way relationships, per the error string "use 'target_entity_id: ENTITY_ID' for two-way or 'target_entity_ids: [A, B]' for N-way").

The one candidate, `type`, is not a cardinality slot. It accepts ANY string with no validation — `type: MANY_TO_ONE`, `type: many_to_one`, `type: BOGUS_VALUE` and `type: "1:N"` all pass `check model` with "✓ Model valid" — and it is DROPPED on compile. After deploying a model.yaml carrying `type: "1:N"`, the compiled model.json relationship reads in full:
  {"source_entity_id":"CHILD","target_entity_id":"PARENT","name":"BELONGS_TO","definition":"A child belongs to a parent.","description":"...","atomic_context":"CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT"}
No `type`. It never reaches the engine.

And the engine is genuinely cardinality-agnostic, not merely silent about it. Its reader template says so — "DAANA-111: Rewritten from LAG-on-pair (tautological for M:N) to fingerprint-based set change detection. Works uniformly for all cardinalities (1:N and M:N)" — and it treats a child's parents as a SET: it STRING_AGGs all target keys per (source key, eff_tmstp) into a fingerprint and emits rows only when that set changes. I proved the many side is real: CH5 loaded with two parent codes at the SAME extracted_at produced two pair rows AND two view rows for one child, and the view's rank() tie left both at nbr=1.

So the generator cannot learn "many-to-one" from the model, and it cannot learn it from the data either, because the data is legitimately many-to-many. Something else must say it. Three options, none of them in the model file: (a) declare it in dab/uss.yaml, which is ours and already exists for events and measures; (b) derive it from the mapping — a relationship whose `target_transformation_expression` reads a single column of the source entity's own row (mapping rule M5 already forbids subqueries and reaches into other tables, so this expression is structurally single-valued per source row) is many-to-one BY CONSTRUCTION, with the one caveat that the same primary key can appear on several staged rows in one load; or (c) assert it as a data check that fails the build when any child has more than one open pair. (b) plus (c) is the honest pair: infer from the mapping, and pin it with a check, because nothing in the engine will stop a second parent appearing.
result.numberType:
DECIMAL(28,8), in every presentation object, regardless of the source column's declared type. My source column was DECIMAL(12,2).

DESCRIBE dab."view_CHILD"
  CHILD_key                VARCHAR
  CHILD_CODE               VARCHAR
  CHILD_AMOUNT             DECIMAL(28,8)
  CHILD_PLACED_ON          TIMESTAMP

DESCRIBE dab."view_CHILD_hist"
  CHILD_key                VARCHAR
  eff_tmstp                TIMESTAMP
  CHILD_CODE               VARCHAR
  CHILD_AMOUNT             DECIMAL(28,8)
  CHILD_PLACED_ON          TIMESTAMP

Values come back fully scaled: 10.50000000, 20.25000000, 30.00000000, 40.00000000, 50.00000000, 60.00000000.

The cast is explicit in the entity macro, not incidental: `CAST(max(CHILD_AMOUNT) AS DECIMAL(28,8)) AS CHILD_AMOUNT`, and the binary carries the literal type strings "NUMBER(28,8)" / "numeric_ddl" for the other dialects.

Physically a NUMBER lands in the `val_num DECIMAL(28,8)` column of dab.CHILD_desc (a STRING lands in `val_str VARCHAR`, a START_TIMESTAMP in `sta_tmstp TIMESTAMP`, a UNIT in `uom`):
DESCRIBE dab."CHILD_desc" -> CHILD_key VARCHAR | type_key BIGINT | seq_nbr INTEGER | eff_tmstp TIMESTAMP | ver_tmstp TIMESTAMP | row_st VARCHAR | sta_tmstp TIMESTAMP | end_tmstp TIMESTAMP | val_str VARCHAR | val_num DECIMAL(28,8) | uom VARCHAR | uom_type VARCHAR | data_key BIGINT | inst_key BIGINT | inst_row_key BIGINT | popln_tmstp TIMESTAMP
SELECT ... WHERE type_key=2 -> CH1 | 2 | 2026-01-01 00:00:00 | Y | NULL | 10.50000000 | NULL   (val_str NULL, val_num carries it)

This matches ADR 0002's declared bridge type for a sum measure, DECIMAL(28,8), exactly — the generator can cast to it without widening or narrowing anything. Note for the destination: DuckDB hands this to Python as decimal.Decimal, and it renders as "10.50000000" unless formatted.
result.correctQuery:
-- Latest open pair per child, read from the pair TABLE.
-- Verified to run against the probe warehouse; returns exactly one row per child
-- that has any pair (CH1|P2, CH2|P2, CH3|P3, CH4|P1, CH5|P1) and no row for the
-- parentless CH6, which is why the caller must LEFT JOIN to it.
SELECT x.CHILD_key,
       x.PARENT_key,
       x.eff_tmstp
FROM dab."CHILD_PARENT_x" AS x
WHERE x.row_st = 'Y'
  AND x.type_key = (
        SELECT CAST(atom_contx_key AS BIGINT)
        FROM dab__meta.atom_contx_desc
        WHERE val_str = 'CHILD_BELONGS_TO_PARENT'
      )
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
          PARTITION BY x.CHILD_key
          ORDER BY x.eff_tmstp DESC, x.ver_tmstp DESC, x.PARENT_key
        ) = 1
ORDER BY x.CHILD_key

-- Four things in that query are load-bearing:
--   row_st = 'Y'      : the engine writes an 'N' row when the source row disappears
--                       (reproduced), and the pair table keeps both.
--   type_key filter   : the pair table is named for the ENTITY PAIR, not the
--                       relationship, so two relationships between the same two
--                       entities share it. view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT> does NOT filter
--                       type_key, which is a bug waiting for the second relationship.
--   row_number, not rank : rank() is what the engine's own macro uses, and it
--                       returns TWO rows for a child whose source named two parents
--                       at the same timestamp (verified with CH5). row_number plus
--                       the PARENT_key tiebreaker is deterministic.
--   ver_tmstp in ORDER BY : the 'N' soft-delete row shares eff_tmstp with the row
--                       it closes and is separated only by ver_tmstp.

-- For a bridge row the generator wants the pair IN EFFECT AT THE EVENT, not the
-- latest pair. Same table, a different predicate — this is the query that reading
-- the relationship VIEW makes impossible, and the real reason ADR 0002's decision
-- is right. Verified to run; CH1's January row correctly gets P1, not P2:
SELECT c.CHILD_key, c.CHILD_PLACED_ON, c.CHILD_AMOUNT, x.PARENT_key
FROM dab."view_CHILD_hist" AS c
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT CHILD_key, PARENT_key, eff_tmstp, ver_tmstp
  FROM dab."CHILD_PARENT_x"
  WHERE row_st = 'Y' AND type_key = 1
) AS x
  ON x.CHILD_key = c.CHILD_key AND x.eff_tmstp <= c.eff_tmstp
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY c.CHILD_key, c.eff_tmstp
                           ORDER BY x.eff_tmstp DESC, x.ver_tmstp DESC, x.PARENT_key) = 1
ORDER BY c.CHILD_key
-- returns: CH1|2026-01-01|10.50000000|P1   CH2|...|P2   CH3|...|NULL   CH4|...|P1   CH5|...|P1
gotchas: ADR 0002 is WRONG where it says a changed foreign key can drop out of the relationship view entirely. It cannot. The rank partitions by (source key, type_key) and every pair row is row_st='Y', so the child is always present — pointing at its NEWEST parent, with the old pair erased. The failure mode is misattribution of history, not silently missing rows. The decision (read the pair table) is right; the sentence justifying it needs rewriting.

ADR 0002 and the dab skill are BOTH WRONG in the blanket claim that 'view_<entity>_with_rel carries no relationship key columns at all; its column list is byte-identical to view_<entity>'. That is true only on the relationship's SOURCE side. On the TARGET side the macro becomes a double LEFT JOIN and the view gains the source entity's key AND every one of its attributes: DESCRIBE dab.view_PARENT_with_rel -> PARENT_key | PARENT_CODE | PARENT_LABEL | CHILD_key | CHILD_CODE | CHILD_AMOUNT | CHILD_PLACED_ON. For slice 2 (ORDER IS_PLACED_BY CUSTOMER) that means view_ORDER_with_rel stays a passthrough, as the repo believes, but view_CUSTOMER_with_rel becomes a fanned-out order-grained view. The data check that currently asserts 'with_rel carries no relationship key' will still pass on ORDER while being false on CUSTOMER — it needs to name the side it is checking.

view_<target>_with_rel is a LIVE FAN TRAP and the probe demonstrates it: 3 parents produced 6 rows in view_PARENT_with_rel, and sum(CHILD_AMOUNT) over it was 200.75 against the true 150.75 from view_CHILD. This is the fan-out ADR 0002 says the bridge exists to avoid, and it is now available as a one-line mistake in the DAR generator.

The pair table is named for the ENTITY PAIR (<SRC>_<TGT>_x), not the relationship. A second relationship between the same two entities shares that table and is distinguished only by type_key. But view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT> is literally `SELECT * FROM f_<src>_<tgt>_x()` with NO type_key predicate, so with two relationships between the same pair both views would return both relationships' rows and be identical to each other. Read from SQL, not observed (I only declared one relationship). The generator must filter type_key itself.

A foreign key set to NULL is NEVER retracted. Re-landing CH2 with parent_code NULL at a later extracted_at wrote nothing at all: no new row, no tombstone, no row_st flip. The pair table and the view still show the stale CH2|P2. The engine's reader filters `AND target IS NOT NULL`, so 'belongs to nobody' is inexpressible. If Northwind ever nulls a customer on an order, DAB will keep the old customer forever and nothing will say so.

row_st on the pair table goes to 'N' in exactly one case: the SOURCE ROW disappears from das__staged, and FULL_LOG's truedelta DEL branch closes it (reproduced — a second row, same eff_tmstp, later ver_tmstp, row_st='N'). That also removes the entity from view_<E>. In this architecture das__staged is append-only over dlt parquet, so it should never fire — but the generator must still filter row_st='Y', because when it does fire the pair table keeps both rows and an unfiltered read would resurrect a deleted pair.

rank() TIES ARE NOT BROKEN. A child whose source named two parents at the same extracted_at got two pair rows and TWO rows in the relationship view (CH5|P1 and CH5|P2, both eff 2026-04-01). The engine's own macro uses rank(), so the view is not one-row-per-child by construction. A generator that copies the engine's rank() will duplicate bridge rows and double a measure. Use row_number() with an explicit tiebreaker, and add a check that fails the build when any child has more than one open pair.

The presentation views wrap DuckDB TABLE MACROS that take a p_eff_tmstp with a default, so the whole DAB layer is point-in-time queryable for free: f_child_parent_x(TIMESTAMP '2026-01-15') returned CH1|P1 while f_child_parent_x() returned CH1|P2. Same for f_CHILD / f_PARENT. Nothing in the repo's docs mentions this, and it is the cheapest correct way to ask 'who was the parent when the event happened' if you would rather not hand-roll the as-of join.

type_key is NOT stable across models — it was 1 for the relationship here, 17 in the earlier spike, and 2/3/4 for CHILD attributes vs 15/16 for PARENT attributes in the same model. Never hardcode it. Resolve it from dab__meta.atom_contx_desc by val_str = '<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>', and CAST(atom_contx_key AS BIGINT) — the metadata column is VARCHAR while type_key is BIGINT, which is what the engine's own v_* views do.

Relationships work fine under FULL_LOG on BOTH sides. The earlier spike only exercised a relationship whose source used TRANSACTIONAL, so this was untested against the repo's mandated strategy (M3). install/check/deploy/execute all exited 0, and re-execute was idempotent — the pair table only grew when the source actually changed.
<entity>_focal and <entity>_idfr are still created and still empty (0 rows) with a relationship present, so ADR 0002's data check on that still holds.

A NUMBER attribute is DECIMAL(28,8) everywhere and reaches Python as decimal.Decimal rendering as '10.50000000'. It matches ADR 0002's declared sum-measure type exactly, but the marimo page will need explicit formatting or freight will print with eight decimal places.

tensions.rule: ADR 0002: "The generator reads `view_<entity>_hist` and the relationship pair objects, and nothing else" — versus ADR 0004: "DAR reads the `view_*` layer only. Not `_focal`, not `_idfr`, not `_with_rel`."
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: These two records contradict each other and slice 2 is the first slice in which the contradiction has an object to be about. `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x` is a BASE TABLE, not a `view_*` object (spike 2 finding 2 lists it under BASE TABLE alongside `ORDER_desc`). ADR 0002 says read it and explicitly rejects the alternative: "Reading the relationship *views* rather than the pair objects is the subtle one: those views rank pairs by effective timestamp and keep the open rows, and our effective timestamp is the moment DAS observed the row, so a changed foreign key can drop out of the view entirely." ADR 0004 says the opposite, in the record that is meant to be the home for facts about this engine on this platform. `.claude/skills/dab/SKILL.md` reproduces both positions in adjacent bullets ("DAR reads the `view_*` layer only" and "Relationship keys come from `view_<src>_<rel>_<tgt>` or the pair table"). Worse: no spike observed `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x`'s columns, and no spike observed the SQL behind `view_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER` — so ADR 0002's stated reason for rejecting the view is not grounded in anything recorded in spike-findings.json. Whichever object is chosen, the choice is currently being made on an unverified claim.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 3 — change the rule, by superseding. Recommend: slice 2's ADR (0006) settles which DAB object the generator reads for an inherited key, on evidence gathered first (DESCRIBE both objects, and observe what each does when a foreign key changes across two loads), and supersedes ADR 0004's sentence "DAR reads the `view_*` layer only" with the narrower true statement. Recourse 1 is not enough — this is not an ambiguity, it is two records giving opposite instructions — and the §8 exception that allows a record to be corrected in place has closed, because both were written in slice 1.

tensions.rule: ADR 0002's column contract: "`<entity>_key` … one per entity in model order"; and `dar__uss.<entity>` is a peripheral table, one per entity
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: The implementation is narrower than the contract, and slice 2 is where the gap bites. `src/adss/uss.py:entity_keys` computes `touched = {event.entity_id for event in uss.events}` and emits a key column only for entities that own an event. `src/adss/cli.py:_generate` builds peripherals from the same set. CUSTOMER has no event in slice 2 — no customer stage, no customer measure — so as the code stands the generator would emit no `customer_key` column and no `dar__uss.customer` table, and the question would be unanswerable. Neither existing check can see this: `test_the_bridge_column_contract_is_an_order_not_a_set` and `checks.py`'s DESCRIBE comparison both derive what they expect from `bridge_columns()`, the same function that is wrong. `entity_keys`'s own docstring admits the shape of this blind spot for the sibling case of ordering.
tensions.resolution: None of the three recourses applies cleanly — the rule fits and the code does not, so this is a defect, not a rule question. But there is a small rule question inside it that should be settled at the same time by recourse 1 (clarify this page / the ADR): does an entity in the model that no stage can reach get a key column? ADR 0002 read literally says yes ("one per entity"); the USS walk says no (blog *consumption-layer-generates-itself*: "follow any path that never fans out, and inherit everything along it"). Recommend: state the contract as "one key column per entity reachable from any staged entity by the many-to-one walk, in model order — the walk's fixed point, not the event list", fix `entity_keys` and `_generate` to that, and add a machinery test over a neutral two-entity fixture whose expectation is written out by hand rather than derived from `bridge_columns()`.

tensions.rule: §1.2: "No source name appears anywhere in `dab/model.yaml` — not in an id, not in a name, not in a definition, not in a description" (hard rule)
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: Northwind's Customer entity has a `Country` property and its Order entity has a `Freight` property (verified in the OData metadata). Slice 2 needs a country attribute on CUSTOMER and a NUMBER attribute on ORDER for the sum to read. Under the rule's literal text, `CUSTOMER_COUNTRY` and `FREIGHT` both contain a string that is a source column name — `country` and `freight` will both appear as `target_name`s in `das/contracts/*.yaml`. Slice 1 dodged this entirely: `ORDER_NUMBER`, `PLACED_ON` and `DESTINATION_COUNTRY` share no substring with `order_id`, `order_date` or `ship_country`. The document also undercuts its own rule two lines earlier: §1.2's singular-names row illustrates itself with `SHIP_COUNTRY`, which is precisely the mechanical snake_case of Northwind's `ShipCountry` and precisely the name slice 1 refused to use. Note that this bites only `model.yaml`: §1.2's own arbiter sentence says `dab/uss.yaml` is governed by §1.3 and §2, so the measure id `FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT` is not in scope — only the attribute it sums is.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. The rule was aimed at moving a dependency, not at forbidding a word the domain owns; the operative test is whether the name is the *source's coinage for the thing*. `ShipCountry` is Northwind's coinage for a concept the business calls the destination, so renaming it was right. `Country` and `Freight` are the domain's own words that Northwind also happens to use, so keeping them moves no dependency: replace Northwind and the business still calls it the customer's country and the freight it paid. Recommend: add that sentence and a worked example to §1.2, replace the stale `SHIP_COUNTRY` illustration with one that is not a source name, and name the attributes `CUSTOMER_COUNTRY` and `FREIGHT`. Do not invent `BASED_IN_COUNTRY` to dodge the string match — an invented name that exists only to evade a rule is the quiet exception §11 refuses, and it hides the rule question instead of settling it.

tensions.rule: §1.2 guideline: "Descriptive attributes are prefixed with their entity (`CUSTOMER_NAME`, `ORDER_LINE_ID`) … The prefix is what makes an attribute readable once it has been inherited into a wide DAR row"; against §1.3 hard rule: "Attribute columns are the lower-cased attribute identifier, unchanged"
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: Following the guideline gives `CUSTOMER_COUNTRY`, and §1.3 then forces the DAR column to be `dar__uss.customer.customer_country` — a stutter that will be read a hundred times and cannot be shortened. Meanwhile the guideline's stated *reason* does not hold in this architecture: ADR 0002 decided that only keys inherit, so there is no wide DAR row carrying another entity's attributes. Attributes live on per-entity peripherals, where the table name already qualifies them. So the guideline is buying readability against a row shape this system does not build. Cutting the other way: this slice's entire point is that the customer's country and the order's destination country are different countries, and a flat glossary listing `COUNTRY` next to `DESTINATION_COUNTRY` invites exactly the confusion the question exists to expose.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend keeping the prefix (`CUSTOMER_COUNTRY`) and accepting `customer.customer_country`, but rewriting the guideline's *why*, which is currently false here: the prefix earns its keep because attribute identifiers are read in one flat glossary and one flat `defines:` list, not because DAR rows are wide. A guideline whose stated reason does not apply is one a reviewer cannot use to tell a real violation from a case it was never aimed at, which is what §How-to-read-a-rule says the why is for.

tensions.rule: B8 — "Meaning is defined exactly once"; §1.2 — every attribute has a definition; `src/adss/uss.py:read_uss` — every measure has a definition
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: The first sum measure forces two definitions of one number. `ORDER.FREIGHT` needs a definition in `model.yaml`, and `ORDER.measures.FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT` needs one in `uss.yaml`, and both are about the same money. Slice 1 never met this because a count measure sums nothing — `PLACED_ORDERS_COUNT` has no attribute behind it, so its definition had no rival. The failure mode is the one B8 names: the two drift, and the glossary on the page shows one while the bridge computes from the other. Nothing in conventions §1.2 or §2 says how the labour divides.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend adding to §2: the attribute's definition says what the number *is* on one instance ("the charge the business paid the carrier to deliver this order; the source states no currency"); the measure's definition says what *aggregating* it means and over what set ("freight across orders, on the day each order was placed; additive along every dimension the order reaches"). If the measure's definition can be written without repeating the attribute's, they are not two definitions of one thing. Add the split as a worked example beside `revenue_order_lines_amount`, which has the same shape and is already in the table.

tensions.rule: §10: "The staged query reads `das__staged.<table>__current`"; and ADR 0005: "the control query has a shelf life … from the first question spanning two sources … Slice 6 is where that bill arrives"
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: Slice 2's control must join `das__staged.orders__current` to `das__staged.customers__current` on `customer_id`. §10 says `<table>` in the singular and nothing in `check_question` counts tables, so a two-table control passes mechanically — but the convention's text does not say whether it is permitted. And the control now encodes the same decision the DAB relationship encodes: "an order's customer is the one whose CustomerId matches". Independence weakens by exactly that much. ADR 0005's *dating* survives: `docs/questions/README.md` calls slice 6 "**The second source.** A file drop with its own customer identifiers", so "two sources" means two source systems and slice 2 spans two entity sets of one. But ADR 0005's *reason* — "reimplementing DAB inside the check" — starts being paid here, one join early, and the record does not say so.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend: §10 gains a sentence saying the control may read more than one `__current` view and may join them on the source's own declared referential constraint, because that is still the source's vocabulary and not DAB's; and that the moment the control needs identity *resolution* rather than a declared foreign key, it has stopped being independent and the arrangement is over. Slice 2's ADR should record honestly that the shelf life started running one slice earlier than ADR 0005 predicted, and what remains of the check's value: it still catches a dropped row, a multiplied measure and a mis-inherited key, which are precisely slice 2's three risks.

tensions.rule: §10 / ADR 0005 — the answer query reads `dar__uss` and nothing else; ADR 0002 — keys inherit along many-to-one relationships
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: Nothing forbids `uss.sql` joining two peripherals to each other. If the model gave ORDER a `CUSTOMER_NUMBER` attribute, the answer query could read `_bridge` → `dar__uss."order"` (INNER, own key) → `dar__uss.customer` on `o.customer_number = c.customer_number`, never touch `customer_key`, and pass every existing check: `check_question` only looks for forbidden schema prefixes. The relationship would be modelled, deployed and inherited, and the slice would demonstrate none of it. This is the invisible way to fake slice 2, and it is one attribute away.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend a new hard rule in §10 or §1.3: an answer query joins each peripheral to the bridge on that entity's key column, never a peripheral to another peripheral; and a foreign key is never modelled as an attribute of the referring entity, because that is a second expression of a relationship the model already declares (M5's why already says every join must come from a declared relationship, but says it only about mapping expressions). Both halves are cheaply checkable in `check_question`.

tensions.rule: `.claude/skills/destination/SKILL.md`: "Cast an aggregate to `DOUBLE` before charting: DuckDB `DECIMAL` reaches the frontend as a decimal type the chart library cannot encode" — against ADR 0005: "the page reads the question's own `uss.sql`" and `src/adss/checks.py`: `control == answer` on Python tuples
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: Slice 1's measure is a count and `uss.sql` casts it to `BIGINT`, so this never arose. The first sum returns `DECIMAL(38, 8)` from the star schema and `DECIMAL(38, 4)` from the source; `Decimal` comparison is by value, so those agree. But if the DOUBLE cast is put inside `uss.sql` to satisfy the chart, the acceptance check compares a `float` against a `Decimal`, and in Python `Decimal('32.38') == 32.38` is False for most values — the question would go red with a difference nobody can see in the numbers as printed.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend: §10 or the destination skill states that the cast for charting happens in the page, over the returned frame, never in `uss.sql` — because `uss.sql` is run verbatim by both the page and the check, and a presentation concern in it changes what the check compares. Keep `uss.sql` returning DECIMAL; cast in `destinations/app.py` on the polars frame.

tensions.rule: §1.4 M6 — "its target expression mirrors the target entity's own key expression exactly"; and `src/adss/mapping.py:check_mapping(mapping)`, which sees one mapping at a time
tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: M6's third clause is a constraint between two files: the relationship's `target_transformation_expression` in `order-mapping.yaml` must mirror `customer-mapping.yaml`'s `primary_keys[0]`. `check_mapping` takes a single `Mapping` and cannot express it, and `read_mapping` does not parse `relationships:` at all. Separately, "exactly" reads as byte-identical text, but the two expressions are evaluated against *different tables* — here they coincide only because Northwind spells the foreign key `CustomerId` on Orders and the key `CustomerId` on Customers, so both become `customer_id`. A future slice whose foreign key has a different column name makes the literal reading impossible to satisfy.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page. Recommend: restate M6's third clause as "the same transformation, applied to the referring table's own foreign-key column" — the shape must match (bare column against bare column, `cast(... AS VARCHAR)` against `cast(... AS VARCHAR)`), the column name need not — and note that the `source_table` clause remains byte-identical because that one really is the same string. Then give the checker the whole set of mappings so it can enforce it, and land the failing test in the same commit.

tensions.howSliceTwoStrainsIt: The fan trap ADR 0002 argues about is a *measure* being copied down an edge. Slice 2 creates a second one it does not discuss: the generator's own join. The `order` stage CTE must acquire `CUSTOMER_key` from the pair object, and if that object holds more than one row per order — which it will the moment an order's customer changes across two loads, since the pair carries `eff_tmstp` (spike 2 finding 4) — the stage multiplies, and `sum(_measure__order__freight_orders_amount)` doubles with no error. The same join, done as INNER instead of LEFT, silently *drops* every order with no customer and shrinks the total. Both failures are in the generator, one level below the rule that is written down (which is about the reader's query), and no rule covers either.
tensions.resolution: Recourse 1 — clarify this page, once slice 2's ADR has decided it. Recommend the generator-side rule be stated in §1.3 alongside the reader-side one: the stage's join to a relationship object is LEFT and must be proved one-to-at-most-one — the object is reduced to one row per source key by latest `eff_tmstp` before it is joined — because an inheritance join that fans out multiplies the owning stage's measure exactly as copying it would. The good news is that slice 1's own acceptance check is the regression guard for the fan-out half: q01 counts orders off the same stage, so a multiplied stage turns q01 red as well as q02. The dropped-row half has no such guard, because the recording contains no order without a customer.

result.theJoinOnPaper:
"WHICH STAGE OWNS THE MEASURE. The `order` stage, on the `placed` event. Freight is a NUMBER on ORDER (one charge per order), and `src/adss/uss.py` requires a sum measure to name an attribute of the event's own entity — `_stage_cte` emits `cast(placed."FREIGHT" AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS _measure__order__freight_orders_amount` reading `dab."view_ORDER_hist"`. There is no alternative: CUSTOMER has no freight attribute, and a CUSTOMER stage carrying freight would be the fan trap written down as a design. Slice 2 therefore adds no stage — the bridge still has exactly one branch, one row per order whose PLACED_ON is set, and gains one measure column appended after `_measure__order__placed_orders_count`.

WHICH KEY IS INHERITED. `customer_key`, onto the `order` stage, along ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER — many orders, one customer, so the edge is many-to-one and the walk may cross it (blog *the-consumption-layer-generates-itself*: "follow any path that never fans out, and inherit everything along it"). Never the reverse: `order_key` must not propagate to a customer stage, and there is no customer stage in slice 2 anyway. The bridge's key columns become (`order_key`, `customer_key`) in that order — model order, which means CUSTOMER must be APPENDED after ORDER in `dab/model.yaml` or the published contract is rearranged rather than extended (ADR 0002, blueprint B7).

Two code facts make this more than a declaration. `entity_keys()` currently scopes key columns to entities that own an event, and `_generate()` scopes peripherals the same way; CUSTOMER owns no event, so as the code stands there would be neither a `customer_key` column nor a `dar__uss.customer` table. Both must become walk-scoped before any of the rest is possible.

THE GENERATOR'S OWN JOIN — the decision below the documented rule. The `placed` CTE must acquire `CUSTOMER_key` from the relationship object. Two properties are required and neither is written down anywhere: (1) the join is LEFT, or an order with no customer disappears from the bridge and its freight leaves the grand total silently; (2) the relationship object must be reduced to one row per ORDER_key — latest `eff_tmstp` — before the join, or the stage multiplies and `sum(freight)` doubles. The pair carries `eff_tmstp` and `ver_tmstp` (spike 2 finding 4), so more than one row per order is a live possibility the moment a customer id changes across two loads. ADR 0002's fan-trap argument is about measures being copied down an edge; it does not cover a key-inheritance join that fans out, which produces the same wrong number by a different route.

THE ANSWER QUERY. Three references, and the joins are decided one at a time:

  FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
  INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key
  LEFT JOIN dar__uss.customer AS c ON b.customer_key = c.customer_key
  WHERE b._event = 'placed'
  GROUP BY cal.quarter_label, c.customer_country
  ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country

`_calendar` — INNER. `_event_date` is the row's own date, non-null by the column contract, and the calendar is generated dense and daily from `min(_event_date)` to `max(_event_date)` over the bridge itself, so every event date has a calendar row by construction. Note this join is on a date, not a key: ADR 0002's INNER/LEFT rule is about keys and does not literally cover it; INNER is right here for the reason just given, not by appeal to that rule.

`customer` — LEFT, and this is the rule going live. `customer_key` is INHERITED on the `order` stage, not the stage's own key, so ADR 0002 and the dar skill both require LEFT. An INNER join would drop every order whose customer key is null and shrink the freight total — the exact "routing a number through the layers changed it" failure the acceptance check exists to catch, arriving through the query rather than the pipeline.

`dar__uss."order"` — not joined at all. The question needs no ORDER attribute: freight is a measure on the bridge, the quarter comes from the calendar, the country comes from CUSTOMER. If a later question needs one, that join is INNER, because `order_key` is the row's own stage key.

WHAT THE LEFT JOIN COSTS AND WHY IT IS STILL RIGHT. In the recording it costs nothing and buys nothing: all 830 order records carry a non-null CustomerId across 89 distinct values, so LEFT and INNER return identical rows and the acceptance check cannot tell them apart. That is the uncomfortable part — slice 2's headline rule is unenforced by slice 2's own data. Three things fix it: a machinery test over a neutral fixture with a dangling child that asserts the generated stage CTE uses a LEFT join; a data check comparing `sum(_measure__order__freight_orders_amount)` over the whole bridge against `sum(freight)` over `das__staged.orders__current WHERE order_date IS NOT NULL`, which catches both a dropped row and a multiplied one independent of any grouping; and a check that the count of bridge rows with a null `customer_key` equals the count of orders whose customer is absent from `customers__current`.

THE CONTROL QUERY MUST MIRROR IT, ONE JOIN AT A TIME.

  FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o
  LEFT JOIN das__staged.customers__current AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY strftime(o.order_date, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(o.order_date) AS VARCHAR), c.country

LEFT, for the same reason and stated as the same reason — slice 1's question file set the precedent of writing down that both queries take the same position deliberately rather than by coincidence. `WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL` mirrors the stage's own `WHERE placed."PLACED_ON" IS NOT NULL`; without it the control counts freight the bridge cannot hold, and this matters more for a sum than it did for slice 1's count, because a reader may reconcile the total against the source's total freight. The quarter label must be composed to match `_calendar.quarter_label` exactly ('1996-Q3'), which is `strftime('%Y') || '-Q' || quarter()` in the generator.

THE TWO EDGE CASES, AND WHETHER THE QUESTION HAS TO SAY.

An order with no customer — null CustomerId, or a CustomerId absent from the Customers recording. Bridge row exists, freight present, `customer_key` null; LEFT join yields a null country; the freight lands in a null-country group in BOTH queries and they agree. The generator never invents a member (§1.3), so there is no 'Unknown' row and no `coalesce`. THE QUESTION HAS TO SAY — §1.3 puts the choice in the question file explicitly, and slice 1's `## Nulls` section is the precedent. Neither case occurs in the orders recording (zero null CustomerIds in 830 records), and whether any of the 89 customer ids is absent from Customers cannot be known until `adss das record --contract customers` has run — so the question must state the position, and the slice must actually check the dangling case rather than assume it away.

A customer with no orders. Peripheral row exists; no bridge row anywhere, because there is no customer stage and no order points at them. The query drives from `_bridge`, so that customer never appears — and neither does their country, unless another customer in it ordered. Both queries behave identically, so the check stays green. This is correct for the question as asked: no order means no freight, and a zero row would require a RIGHT or FULL join the architecture does not offer and the question does not ask for. NO RULE REQUIRES THE QUESTION TO SAY — this is a consequence of the grain, not a null-handling choice. But one sentence is worth writing anyway, because "why is Poland missing?" is the first thing the logistics manager will ask, and the honest answer is that no customer there has ever ordered."

ADR 0002 instructs the generator to read this object, so the record depends on a shape nobody has looked at.

ADR 0002's reason for rejecting the relationship VIEW is not backed by any spike observation. The record says those views "rank pairs by effective timestamp and keep the open rows, [so] a changed foreign key can drop out of the view entirely". No spike captured the view's SQL definition, and no spike changed a foreign key across two loads. This is the argument that decides which DAB object the generator reads, and it is currently reasoned rather than observed.

No relationship has ever been observed loading under the configuration this repository mandates. Spike 2's ORDER mapping used `ingestion_strategy: TRANSACTIONAL` with `batch_expression: ingested_at` and `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: order_date` — both forbidden here by M3 and M4. So the only evidence that `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x` is populated at all comes from a configuration conventions §1.4 refuses. Whether the pair object is produced correctly under `FULL_LOG` + `extracted_at` is untested by anything.

What the engine does with a null or dangling foreign key is unknown. Does `target_transformation_expression: customer_id` evaluating to NULL produce no pair row, or a pair row with a null CUSTOMER_key? Does a customer id that exists on the order but in no customer record produce a pair row pointing at a CUSTOMER_key that has no `_desc` rows? Neither was exercised — spike 2's three orders all had valid customers. Both cases change what the bridge holds.

Whether daana's model-level relationship block accepts an `id` key is unknown. The documented shape (blog `doc-ch1.txt`) is `name: IS_PLACED_BY` with `source_entity_id` and `target_entity_id` and no `id`, but conventions §1.2 requires that "entity, attribute and relationship identifiers are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, with `id` and `name` holding the identical string". If the schema has no `id` key for a relationship, that clause cannot be satisfied and needs clarifying; if it does, nothing has confirmed it.

Nothing establishes how many customers Northwind has or whether any has no orders. 89 distinct CustomerIds appear across the 830 recorded orders; the Customers recording does not exist yet. Whether the 89 are a strict subset of the customers, and whether any recorded customer id on an order is absent from Customers, are both determinable only after `adss das record --contract customers` runs — and both change what the question's null section has to say.

No rule exists for the generator's own inheritance join. Conventions and ADR 0002 state the INNER/LEFT rule for the *reader's* query only. That the stage's join to the relationship object must be LEFT, and must be reduced to one row per source key before joining, is nowhere written — and both failures are silent (a shrunk total, a doubled total).

No rule forbids an answer query joining one peripheral to another. `check_question` only checks which schemas are named, so slice 2 could be faked entirely — model an ORDER foreign-key attribute, join `dar__uss."order"` to `dar__uss.customer` on it, and never touch the inherited key — while every test and check stays green.

No rule says how a NUMBER attribute in `model.yaml` is named relative to the §2 measure that sums it, nor how their two definitions divide the labour. §2 governs measure ids in `uss.yaml`; §1.2 governs attribute ids in `model.yaml`; nothing connects them, and the first sum makes them adjacent.

No rule says what `effective_timestamp:` should be for a new attribute. `src/adss/model.py` does not read the key at all — it is engine-only configuration — and neither conventions nor the dab skill mentions it, yet slice 2 adds several attributes and will pick values for all of them silently. The existing model has `false` on ORDER_NUMBER, `true` on DESTINATION_COUNTRY, and nothing on the START_TIMESTAMP; the neutral fixture uses `true` for its NUMBER attribute.

Nothing says where the DOUBLE cast for charting belongs. The destination skill says to cast aggregates to DOUBLE; ADR 0005 says the page runs `uss.sql` verbatim; `checks.py` compares result tuples with `==`. Put the cast in the query and the first sum measure fails the acceptance check on float-versus-Decimal comparison, with numbers that print identically.

Nothing says what `answer.png` is when one app renders two questions. `docs/questions/01-.../answer.png` is byte-identical to `.screenshots/app.png`, `Project.destination` is a single hardcoded file, and `shoot()` writes one image at a fixed 1800px height. A second question makes the page taller (truncation risk) and makes one screenshot the record for two questions — while ADR 0005 says the picture records what *that* question was accepted on. Whether q01's accepted image is left alone (it should be) and how q02's is produced are both undecided.

The measure has no currency and nothing says what to do about it. Northwind's Freight carries no currency property, and the engine's type vocabulary has a `UNIT` type for exactly this (daana's own example pairs `order_value_amount` with `order_value_currency`). S1 forbids inventing one in DAS. So the honest move is a definition that records the absence — but no rule says a money measure must state its currency or say that the source does not, and §2's unit slot (`amount`) does not carry it.

result.argument:
**Why the direction is not declared anywhere.**

The tempting move is to declare cardinality where a reader would look for it, in `dab/model.yaml`. It cannot be done. `daana-cli lint` rejects `cardinality:` outright and, in rejecting it, prints the entire grammar: *"Valid fields are: name, definition, description, source, target, source_entity_id, target_entity_id, type"*. The one candidate on that list, `type`, is not a cardinality slot. It accepts `MANY_TO_ONE`, `1:N`, `M:N`, `BANANA` and `42` with exit 0 and no message, and it is dropped on compile: I added `type: "MANY_TO_ONE"` to a two-entity probe model, ran `daana-cli deploy`, and the compiled `model.json` relationship object came back as `{source_entity_id, target_entity_id, name, definition, description, atomic_context}` with the string `MANY_TO_ONE` appearing nowhere in the file, and the generated `f_CHILD_PARENT_x` macro byte-identical to the run without it. A field that lints clean, means nothing, and evaporates is worse than no field: it reads to a human as a statement the system acts on.

That kills the model. The second option, a `cardinality:` block in `dab/uss.yaml`, is genuinely attractive and I nearly took it. `uss.yaml` is already chartered for exactly this — its own header says it holds "what the generated star schema needs to know that the business model does not otherwise say" — and a declaration is checkable before the build rather than after. It loses on two counts. First, it would be a second statement of something the mapping already fixes: a relationship's `target_transformation_expression` reads one row of a table keyed by the source entity (M5 forbids a subquery, an aggregate or a reach into another table), so a source row yields at most one target, and the direction of the name is already a hard rule — §1.2 requires `<SOURCE>_<NAME>_<TARGET>` to read as a sentence precisely because "direction is the thing people get wrong". Second, and decisively, with exactly one relationship in the model there is no second case against which to judge the vocabulary, which is the situation ADR 0001 says to refuse to abstract in. A declaration whose only value is the day a non-`many_to_one` edge exists should be written on that day.

The third option, deriving cardinality from the data at build time, inverts the authority. Data would be telling the model what the business means, and it cannot tell "one target per source by design" from "one target per source because the recording is small". But it is an excellent *check*, and that is where it goes.

So: the direction comes from the declared edge, the justification is the mapping's grammar plus the naming rule, and the data is the confirmation, not the source.

**Why the generator enforces the cardinality rather than trusting it.**

The strongest part of this decision is that the declaration is not load-bearing for the total. The stage's key read is deduplicated with `row_number()` partitioned by the source key, so it emits exactly one row per source key whatever the data does. If the edge turns out not to be many-to-one, the bridge does not multiply; it attributes one row to one of several targets and the check says so. That degrades the failure from a wrong total (invisible, and invisible in *both* of a question's acceptance queries if both are written the same way) to a wrong breakdown with a failing check beside it.

**Which object to read, settled by measurement.**

ADR 0002 said "the relationship pair objects" without saying which, and the engine offers four that disagree. I built the same bridge shape four ways over a probe whose truth is 6 rows and 210.75:

| read | rows | sum |
|---|---|---|
| stage alone (the truth) | 6 | 210.75 |
| `INNER JOIN` the raw pair table | 7 | **211.25** |
| `INNER JOIN dab.view_<REL>` | **6** | **200.75** |
| `LEFT JOIN` the deduplicated `v_<REL>` | 6 | 210.75 |

The middle two are the whole argument. The raw pair table is historized, so a re-pointed key duplicates its row — and the error lands 0.24% high, small enough that nobody looks. The engine's own presentation view gives the *right row count* and the wrong money: it ranks with `rank()`, not `row_number()`, so a source key with two targets at one instant survives twice, and a key that never had a pair is dropped entirely. A row-count check passes. That is the worst failure shape this repository can produce.

`dab."v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>"` is the pair table joined to `dab__meta.atom_contx_desc` to add a `rel_name` column, with no ranking of its own. It is therefore the pair object ADR 0002 meant, with the relationship named instead of numbered. That naming matters more than it looks: the pair table is `<SRC>_<TGT>_x`, named from the *entity pair*, and its own view definition does not filter by relationship, so two edges between the same ordered pair of entities land in one table separated only by a `type_key` that is assigned at deploy and is not stable (1 in one probe, 17 in another). `WHERE edge.rel_name = 'ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER'` says what is meant and costs one predicate.

**Where I differ from the record already in the tree, and what decides it.**

`docs/adr/0006` resolves the pair *as of the stage row's `_observed_at`* — `AND revision._observed_at >= pair.eff_tmstp`. Its reasoning is good: state the rule at the level of a bridge row so it survives a snapshot stage. But `_observed_at` is the *start* of a version's validity, not an instant at which the whole row is observed, and on a transaction stage the version kept is always the latest, whose validity is open-ended. Resolving at the start of an open-ended interval reads the world as it was when the entity's *attributes* last changed — and the engine writes no new entity version when only a foreign key moves, because only changed attribute values get a new `_desc` row. I ran both rules over the same probe:

- latest pair: CH1→P2, CH2→P2, **CH3→P3**, CH4→P1, CH5→P1, CH6→null. Null group 60.00.
- as of `_observed_at`: **CH1→P1**, CH2→P2, **CH3→null**, CH4→P1, CH5→P1, CH6→null. Null group 90.00, and **P3 vanishes from the answer entirely**.

CH3 acquired its parent at 2026-03-01 in a load that changed nothing else, so its entity version stayed at 2026-01-01 and the as-of rule cannot see the pair that exists. CH1 keeps a parent the source has since retracted. The total is 210.75 either way — the left join protects it — but a whole target disappears from the breakdown, which is exactly the "right total, wrong breakdown" failure the rest of this record is spent avoiding.

The rule that keeps both properties is: **resolve as of the end of the version's validity interval.** On a transaction stage that end is open, so it reduces to the latest pair, and the pair CTE is independent of the stage — one CTE per edge rather than one per (stage, edge), which is also the shape that stays readable when three stages walk the same edge. When a snapshot stage arrives and a row's interval has a right end, that slice computes it and this clause is where it lands.

**How far the walk goes.**

ADR 0001 says build for this slice; ADR 0002 published a contract that says keys inherit. Both hold if the *contract* is defined by the walk's reach from the start while the *walk* stays as short as the evidence. So: `entity_keys()` and the peripheral set stop being derived from `uss.events` and become "every entity the declarations touch **or reach**". That is not optional — today `entity_keys()` reads `{event.entity_id for event in uss.events}` and `_generate()` builds peripherals from the same set, so CUSTOMER, which has no event, would get neither a key column nor a `dar__uss.customer` table, and the question could not be answered at all. One definition of reach now decides three things at once: which key columns exist, which peripherals exist, and which joins must be `LEFT`.

The walk itself is one hop, unbounded in breadth. Breadth is judgeable today — the neutral fixture already has two edges from one entity, one of them to an entity with no event — and each edge is another CTE and another left join, composed, with no new decision. Depth is not judgeable: a chain raises cycles, diamonds where two paths reach one entity, and whether the second hop joins from the first hop's key or from its own pair set, and I would be deciding all three blind. So a second hop is a refusal, with the message naming what the slice that needs it must decide, and a `bad_two_hop_walk.yaml` fixture asserting the refusal — which is how this repository already defers (`bad_snapshot_event.yaml`, `bad_sum_of_a_string.yaml`). The refusal is the deferral, and it is tested rather than remembered.

**The fan-out line.**

The measure rule needs no change: `_branch()` already emits `cast(NULL AS <type>)` for every measure a branch does not own, and slice 1 tested it. What slice 2 adds is the guarantee that makes it worth anything — that a stage emits one row per source key after inheriting. And slice 2 *can* demonstrate a multiplication for the first time, which the brief did not expect: not across grains, but across the relationship's own history. Two of the four reads above multiply a measure on a strictly many-to-one edge.

What is still deferred is exactly what ADR 0002 deferred: a parent's measure multiplied across its children. ORDER and CUSTOMER are the same grain here and CUSTOMER owns no measure, so nothing can multiply across the edge however the join is written. D-0001 is now half discharged and the register should say so rather than quietly reading as satisfied.

**The uncomfortable part.**

None of this is testable by the slice's own acceptance query. The recording has 830 orders, none with a null `CustomerId`, all 89 referenced customers present — and `ShipCountry` equals the customer's `Country` for every single order. So a `uss.sql` that grouped by `order.destination_country` and never touched the relationship would produce byte-identical output to the correct one and pass. The reconciliation this system rests on is blind to the thing this slice exists to build, and the confidence has to come from the fixture and the three data checks instead. Saying that is not a caveat; it is the reason the confirmation section is shaped the way it is.

result.contextAndProblem:
Slice 1 built a bridge with one entity and no edges. ADR 0002 justified one shared bridge on a walk over many-to-one relationships — "a stage carries the key of every entity it reaches by walking many-to-one edges" — and admitted in as many words that the walk had zero edges and the property was "asserted here and first exercised in slice 2". This is that slice. The question groups the freight of an order by the *customer's* country, which exists nowhere on the order, so `customer_key` has to arrive on an order row or the question cannot be answered at all.

The first difficulty is that the modelling language has no way to say a relationship is many-to-one, and the generator therefore cannot walk "many-to-one edges" without being told something the model does not say. `daana-cli lint` rejects a `cardinality:` field and, in rejecting it, prints the whole grammar: name, definition, description, source, target, source_entity_id, target_entity_id, type. The only candidate, `type`, accepts any string without validation and is dropped on compile — a model declaring `type: "MANY_TO_ONE"` deploys to byte-identical database objects and produces a compiled `model.json` in which the string does not appear. The vendor's own artefacts disagree about direction as well: the shipped model template's example is `PLACES` with source CUSTOMER and target ORDER, the one-to-many direction, while the tutorial's is `IS_PLACED_BY` with source ORDER and target CUSTOMER, the many-to-one one. A convention the tool's own template contradicts will be broken by whoever copies the template.

The second difficulty is that the engine offers four objects to take the key from, they disagree, and their names do not say which is which. The pair table `<SRC>_<TGT>_x` is historized and named from the entity pair rather than the relationship, so it holds every version of every edge between those two entities, told apart only by a `type_key` assigned at deploy and not stable between models. The presentation view `view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is a macro that ranks with `rank()` — not `row_number()` — and filters `row_st = 'Y'`, so it keeps both sides of a tie and applies an as-of rule of the vendor's choosing. `v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is the pair table joined to the engine's metadata to add a `rel_name` column, unranked and unfiltered. And `view_<entity>_with_rel` carries relationship keys on the target side only, fanned out, despite ADR 0002 recording that it carries none.

The third difficulty is that the failure this slice can cause is invisible. The bridge's whole value is that `sum()` is right, and both ways of getting it wrong here are quiet. Reading the pairs without deduplicating multiplies a measure by the number of times a foreign key was ever restated. Joining `INNER` drops an order whose customer is unknown, taking its freight with it. Neither raises an error, and on a probe with a true total of 210.75 over six rows the first returns 211.25 over seven rows and the second returns 200.75 over six — the right row count and the wrong money.

The fourth difficulty is that slice 2's own data cannot detect any of this. The recording holds 830 orders, none with a null `CustomerId`, every referenced customer present, and — the part that matters — `ShipCountry` equal to the customer's `Country` for all 830. The two countries are different concepts and the model keeps them apart, but on this recording they never disagree, so an answer query that ignored the relationship entirely and grouped by the order's own destination country would produce identical output and pass the reconciliation. Whatever confidence this slice earns has to be earned somewhere other than its own acceptance test.

Finally, the contract itself is at stake, not just the SQL. `entity_keys()` today derives the bridge's key columns from `{event.entity_id for event in uss.events}`, and `_generate()` builds one peripheral per evented entity. CUSTOMER has no event and never will have one in this slice, so under the current rule it gets neither a `customer_key` column nor a `dar__uss.customer` table. The published column contract has to be redefined in terms of what the walk *reaches*, not what the events *touch*, before any of the join work matters.
